fixes.target: appendix-2-table-1: ACMs in buildings listed in order of ease of fibre release

columns: Ease of fibre release and product names
rows: Bulk loose fill, bulk fibre-filled mattresses, quilts and blankets. Also ‘jiffy bag’ type products used for sound insulation.

Bulk loose fill insulation is now rarely found but may be encountered unexpectedly, eg DIY loft insulation and fire-stop packing around cables between floors. Mattresses and quilts used for thermal insulation of industrial boilers were filled with loose asbestos. Paper bags/sacks were also loose-filled and used for sound insulation under floors and in walls.
Usually pure asbestos except for lining/bag. Mattresses and quilts usually contain crocidolite or chrysotile. Acoustic insulation may contain crocidolite or chrysotile.
Loose asbestos may readily become airborne if disturbed. If dry, these materials can give rise to high exposures. Covers may deteriorate or be easily damaged by repair work or accidental contact.
Dry applied, wet applied and trowelled finish.

Thermal and anti-condensation insulation on underside of roofs and sometimes sides of industrial buildings and warehouses. Acoustic insulation in theatres, halls etc. Fire protection on steel and reinforced concrete beams/columns and on underside of floors. Overspray of target areas is common.

Sprayed coatings usually contain 55%–85% asbestos with a Portland cement binder. Crocidolite was the major type until 1962. Mixture of types including crocidolite until mid–1971. Asbestos spray applications were used up to 1974.

The surface hardness, texture and ease of fibre release will vary significantly depending on a number of factors. Sprays have a high potential for fibre release if unsealed, particularly if knocked or the surface is abraded or delaminates from the underlying surface. Dust released may then accumulate on false ceilings, wiring and ventilation systems. ‘Limpet’ (also used for non-asbestos sprays).
Hand-applied thermal lagging, pipe and boiler lagging, pre-formed pipe sections, slabs, blocks. Also tape, rope, corrugated paper, quilts, felts, and blankets.
Thermal insulation of pipes, boilers, pressure vessels, calorifiers etc.

All types of asbestos have been used. Crocidolite used in lagging until 1970. Amosite was phased out by the manufacturers during the 1970s. Content varies 6-85%. Various ad hoc mixtures were hand-applied on joints and bends and pipe runs. Pre-formed sections were widely used, eg ‘85% magnesia’ contained 15% amosite, ‘Caposil’ calcium silicate slabs and blocks contained 8–30% amosite while ‘Caposite’ sections contained ~ 85% amosite. Blankets, felts, papers, tapes and ropes were usually ~100% chrysotile.

The ease of fibre release often depends on the type of lagging used and the surface treatment. Often it will be encapsulated with calico and painted (eg PVA, EVA, latex, bitumen or proprietary polymer emulsions or PVC, neoprene solutions), eg ‘Decadex’ finish is a proprietary polymer emulsion. A harder chemical-/weatherresistant finish is known as ‘Bulldog’.
‘Millboard’ was used for general heat insulation and fire protection. Also used for insulation of electrical equipment and plant.
Crocidolite was used in some millboard manufacture between 1896 and 1965; usually chrysotile. Millboards may contain 37–97% asbestos, with a matrix of clay and starch.
Asbestos ‘Millboard’ has a high asbestos content and low density so is quite easy to break and the surface is subject to abrasion and wear.

Used for fire protection, thermal and acoustic insulation, resistance to moisture movement and general building board. Found in service ducts, firebreaks, infill panels, partitions and ceilings (including ceiling tiles), roof underlay, wall linings, soffits, external canopies and porch linings.

Crocidolite used for some boards up to 1965, amosite up to 1980, when manufacture ceased. Usually 15–25% amosite or a mixture of amosite and chrysotile in calcium silicate. Older boards and some marine boards contain up to 40% asbestos.

AIB can be readily broken, giving significant fibre release. Also significant surface release is possible by abrasion, but surface is usually painted or plastered. Sawing and drilling will also give significant releases. ‘Asbestolux’, ‘Turnasbestos’, ‘LDR’, ‘asbestos wallboard’, ‘insulation board’. Marine boards known as ‘Marinite’ or ‘Shipboard’.
Insulating board in cores and linings of composite products.

Found in fire doors, cladding infill panels, domestic boiler casings, partition and ceiling panels, oven linings and suspended floor systems. Used as thermal insulation and sometimes as acoustic attenuators.
Crocidolite used for some boards up to 1965, amosite up to 1980, when manufacture ceased. 16–40% amosite or a mixture of amosite and chrysotile.
Can be broken by impact; significant surface release possible by abrasion, but usually painted or plastered. Sawing and drilling will also give significant releases. ‘Asbestolux’. Caposil.

Used for electrical/heat insulation of electrical equipment. Also used in some air-conditioning systems as insulation and acoustic lining. Asbestos paper has also been used to reinforce bitumen and other products and as a facing/lining to flooring products, combustible boards, flame-resistant laminate. Corrugated cardboard has been used for duct and pipe insulation.

Asbestos paper can contain ~100% chrysotile asbestos but may be incorporated as a lining, facing or reinforcement for other products, eg roofing felt and damp-proof courses, steel composite wall cladding and roofing (see asbestos bitumen products below), vinyl flooring. Asbestos paper is also sometimes found under MMMF insulation on steam pipes.

Paper materials, if not encapsulated/combined within vinyl, bitumen, or bonded in some way, can easily be damaged and release fibres when subject to abrasion or wear (eg worn flooring surface with paper backing). Asbestos paper, asbestos felt, ‘Novilon’ flooring, Durasteel laminates, vinyl asbestos tile, roofing felt and damp-proof course etc. Pax felt’. ‘Viceroy’ (foil-coated paper). ‘Serval’.
Used as lagging on pipes (see above), jointing and packing materials and as heat/fire-resistant boiler, oven and flue sealing. Caulking in brickwork. Plaited asbestos tubing in electric cable.

Crocidolite and chrysotile were widely used due to length and flexibility of fibres. Other types of asbestos have occasionally been used in the past. Chrysotile alone since at least 1970. Asbestos content approaching 100% unless combined with other fibres.

Weaving reduces fibre release from products, but abrading or cutting the materials will release fibres, likely to degrade if exposed, becoming more friable with age. If used with caulking, fibres will be encapsulated and less likely to be released.

Thermal insulation and lagging (see above), including fire-resisting blankets, mattresses, protective curtains, gloves aprons and overalls. Curtains, gloves etc were sometimes aluminised to reflect heat.
All types of asbestos were used. Since the mid-1960s the vast majority have been chrysotile. Asbestos content approaching 100%.
Fibres may be released if material is abraded.
Used widely in domestic and industrial plant and pipe systems ranging from hot water boilers to industrial power and chemical plant.

Variable but usually around 90% asbestos, crocidolite used for acid resistance and chrysotile for chlor-alkali. Some gasket materials continued to be used after asbestos prohibition in 1999 (through exemption).
May be dry and damage easily when removed. Mainly a problem for maintenance workers. ‘Klingerit’, ‘Lion jointing’, ‘Permanite’, ‘CAF’ – compressed asbestos fibre or ‘It’ in German gaskets.
Used for sealing hot water radiators.
Transport, machinery and lifts, used for brakes and clutch plates.
30–70% chrysotile asbestos bound in phenolic resins. Used up to November 1999.

Normal handling will produce low emissions. Minor emissions when braking. Dust may build up with friction debris. Grinding brake and clutch components to fit and brushing or blowing clean can produce significant peak airborne levels.
Low friability, except when worn to expose textile.
Roofing, wall cladding. Permanent shuttering, cooling tower elements.

10–15% asbestos (some flexible sheets contain a proportion of cellulose). Crocidolite (1950–1969) and amosite (1945–1980) have been used in the manufacture of asbestos cement, although chrysotile (used until November 1999) is by far the most common type found.

Likely to release increasing levels of fibres if abraded, hand sawn or worked on with power tools. Exposed surfaces and acid conditions will remove cement matrix and concentrate unbound fibres on surface and sheet laps. Cleaning asbestos-containing roofs may also release fibres. Asbestos cement, Trafford tile, ‘Bigsix’, ‘Doublesix’, ‘Supersix’, ‘Twin twelve’, ‘Combined sheet’, ‘Glen six’, ‘3’ and 6’ corrugated’, ‘Fort’, ‘Monad’, ‘Troughsec’, ‘Major tile and Canada tile’, ‘Panel sheet’, ‘Cavity decking’.
Semi-compressed flat sheet and partition board.

Partitioning in farm buildings and infill panels for housing, shuttering in industrial buildings, decorative panels for facings, bath panels, soffits, linings to walls and ceilings, portable buildings, propagation beds in horticulture, domestic structural uses, fire surrounds, composite panels for fire protection, weather boarding.
As for profiled sheets. Also 10–25% chrysotile and some amosite for asbestos wood used for fire doors etc. Composite panels contained ~ 4% chrysotile or crocidolite.
Release as for profiled sheets. Flat building sheets, partition board, ‘Poilite’.
Fully compressed flat sheet used for tiles, slates, board.

As above, but where stronger materials are required, and as slates, board cladding, decking and roof slates (eg roller-skating rinks, laboratory worktops). Higher asbestos content sheets produced for industrial applications as a high grade arc and heat-resistant material.
As for profiled sheets. Up to 50% chrysotile.

Release as for profiled sheets. Asbestos-containing roofing slate (eg ‘Eternit’, ‘Turners’, ‘Speakers’), Everite’, ‘Turnall’, ‘Diamond AC’, ‘JM slate’, ‘Glasal AC’, ‘Emalie, Eflex’, ‘Colourglaze’, ‘Thrutone’, ‘Weatherall’, ‘Sindanyo’.
Pre-formed moulded products and extruded products.

Cable troughs and conduits. Cisterns and tanks. Drains and sewer pressure pipes. Fencing. Flue pipes. Rainwater goods. Roofing components (fascias, soffits etc). Ventilators and ducts. Weather boarding. Window sills and boxes, bath panels, draining boards, extraction hoods, copings, promenade tiles etc.
Release as for profiled sheets. ‘Everite’, ‘Turnall’, ‘Promenade tiles’.
Decorative/flexible coatings on walls and ceilings.
3–5% chrysotile asbestos. Chrysotile added up to 1984 but old stock may have been used for several more years. Non-asbestos versions were available from the mid-1970s.
Generally fibres are well contained in the matrix but may be released when old coating is sanded down or scraped off. ‘Artex’, Wondertex’, ‘Suretex’, ‘‘Newtex’, ‘Pebblecoat’, ‘Marblecoat’.

Roofing felts and shingles, semi-rigid asbestos bitumen roofing. Gutter linings and flashings. Bitumen damp-proof courses (DPC). Asbestos/bitumen coatings on metals (eg car body underseals). Bitumen mastics and adhesives (used for floor tiles and wall coverings).

Chrysotile fibre or asbestos paper (approximately 100% asbestos) in bitumen matrix, usually 8% chrysotile. Used up to 1992. Adhesives may contain up to a few per cent chrysotile asbestos. Used up to 1992.
Fibre release unlikely during normal use. Roofing felts, DPC and bitumen-based sealants must not be burnt after removal. See felts and papers.
Thermoplastic floor tiles. PVC vinyl floor tiles and unbacked PVC flooring. Asbestos paper-backed PVC floors. Magnesium oxychloride flooring used in WCs, staircases and industrial flooring.
Up to 25% asbestos. Normally 7% chrysotile. Paper backing approximately 100% chrysotile asbestos. Used up to 1992. About 2% asbestos.

Fibre release is unlikely to be a hazard under normal services conditions. Fibre may be released when material is cut, and there may be substantial release where flooring residue, particularly paper backing, is power-sanded. ‘Novilon’, ‘Serval asbestos’. Very hard, fibre release unlikely.
Used for toilet cisterns, seats, banisters, window seals, lab bench tops.

Plastics usually contain 1-10% chrysotile asbestos. Some amphiboles were used to give improved acid resistance, eg car batteries. Resins were reinforced with woven chrysotile cloth usually contain 20–50% asbestos.
Fibres unlikely to be released, limited emissions during cutting. ‘Siluminite’, ‘Feroasbestos’.
sentences: Bulk loose fill, bulk fibre-filled mattresses, quilts and blankets (loose insulation) are usually pure asbestos except for lining/bag, are now rarely found but may be encountered unexpectedly, eg DIY loft insulation and fire-stop packing around cables between floors, and loose asbestos may readily become airborne if disturbed.

Sprayed coatings (dry applied, wet applied and trowelled finish) were used for thermal and anti-condensation insulation, acoustic insulation and fire protection on steel and reinforced concrete beams/columns, usually contain 55%–85% asbestos, were used up to 1974, and have a high potential for fibre release if unsealed.

Thermal insulation such as hand-applied thermal lagging, pipe and boiler lagging and pre-formed pipe sections is found on pipes, boilers, pressure vessels and calorifiers, may contain all types of asbestos (content varies 6-85%), and its ease of fibre release often depends on the type of lagging used and the surface treatment.
Asbestos ‘Millboard’ was used for general heat insulation and fire protection, may contain 37–97% asbestos, and has a high asbestos content and low density so is quite easy to break.

Insulating board (AIB) was used for fire protection, thermal and acoustic insulation and general building board, usually contains 15–25% amosite or a mixture of amosite and chrysotile, and can be readily broken, giving significant fibre release; sawing and drilling will also give significant releases.

Insulating board in cores and linings of composite products is found in fire doors, cladding infill panels, domestic boiler casings and partition and ceiling panels, contains 16–40% amosite or a mixture of amosite and chrysotile, and can be broken by impact; sawing and drilling will also give significant releases.

Asbestos paper can contain ~100% chrysotile asbestos and was used for electrical/heat insulation of electrical equipment and as a facing/lining to flooring products, and paper materials, if not encapsulated/combined within vinyl, bitumen, or bonded in some way, can easily be damaged and release fibres when subject to abrasion or wear.

Asbestos ropes and yarns were used as lagging on pipes, jointing and packing materials and heat/fire-resistant boiler, oven and flue sealing, have an asbestos content approaching 100% unless combined with other fibres, and abrading or cutting the materials will release fibres.

Asbestos cloth was used for thermal insulation and lagging, including fire-resisting blankets, mattresses, protective curtains, gloves aprons and overalls, has an asbestos content approaching 100%, and fibres may be released if the material is abraded.

Asbestos gaskets and washers are used widely in domestic and industrial plant and pipe systems, are usually around 90% asbestos, and may be dry and damage easily when removed, mainly a problem for maintenance workers.
Asbestos strings were used for sealing hot water radiators and have an asbestos content approaching 100%.

Resin-based friction materials used for brakes and clutch plates in transport, machinery and lifts contain 30–70% chrysotile asbestos, were used up to November 1999, and grinding brake and clutch components to fit and brushing or blowing clean can produce significant peak airborne levels.
Drive belts/conveyor belts in engines and conveyors are chrysotile textiles encapsulated in rubber and have low friability, except when worn to expose textile.

Asbestos cement profiled sheets used for roofing and wall cladding contain 10–15% asbestos, chrysotile (used until November 1999) is by far the most common type found, and they are likely to release increasing levels of fibres if abraded, hand sawn or worked on with power tools.

Semi-compressed flat sheet and partition board (eg partitioning in farm buildings, bath panels, soffits, linings to walls and ceilings, fire surrounds) contains 10–25% chrysotile and some amosite for asbestos wood used for fire doors, and release is as for profiled sheets.

Fully compressed flat sheet used for tiles, slates and board where stronger materials are required is as for profiled sheets, with up to 50% chrysotile in higher asbestos content sheets for industrial applications, and release is as for profiled sheets.

Pre-formed moulded and extruded cement products such as cable troughs, cisterns and tanks, drains and sewer pressure pipes, flue pipes, rainwater goods and window sills are as for profiled sheets, and release is as for profiled sheets.

Textured coatings (decorative/flexible coatings on walls and ceilings) contain 3–5% chrysotile asbestos, chrysotile was added up to 1984, and fibres are generally well contained in the matrix but may be released when old coating is sanded down or scraped off.

Bitumen products such as roofing felts, gutter linings, bitumen damp-proof courses (DPC) and bitumen mastics and adhesives usually contain 8% chrysotile and were used up to 1992; fibre release is unlikely during normal use, and roofing felts, DPC and bitumen-based sealants must not be burnt after removal.

Flooring such as thermoplastic floor tiles (up to 25% asbestos), PVC vinyl floor tiles (normally 7% chrysotile) and asbestos paper-backed PVC floors is unlikely to be a fibre release hazard under normal services conditions, but there may be substantial release where flooring residue, particularly paper backing, is power-sanded.
Reinforced PVC panels and cladding contain 1–10% chrysotile asbestos and fibre release is unlikely.

Reinforced plastic and resin composites used for toilet cisterns, seats, banisters, window seals and lab bench tops usually contain 1-10% chrysotile asbestos (resins reinforced with woven chrysotile cloth usually contain 20–50% asbestos), and fibres are unlikely to be released, with limited emissions during cutting.

fixes.target: appendix-4-table-1: Material assessment algorithm

columns: Examples of scores (see notes for more detail)
rows: Asbestos-reinforced composites (plastics, resins, mastics, roofing felts, vinyl floor tiles, semi-rigid paints or decorative finishes, asbestos cement etc).
AIB, millboards, other low-density insulation boards, asbestos textiles, gaskets, ropes and woven textiles, asbestos paper and felt.
Thermal insulation (eg pipe and boiler lagging), sprayed asbestos, loose asbestos, asbestos mattresses and packing.
Low damage: a few scratches or surface marks, broken edges on boards, tiles etc.
Medium damage: significant breakage of materials or several small areas where material has been damaged revealing loose asbestos fibres.
High damage or delamination of materials, sprays and thermal insulation. Visible asbestos debris.
Composite materials containing asbestos: reinforced plastics, resins, vinyl tiles.
Enclosed sprays and lagging, AIB (with exposed face painted or encapsulated) asbestos cement sheets etc.
Unsealed AIB, or encapsulated lagging and sprays.
sentences: In the material assessment, a product type (or debris from product) of asbestos-reinforced composites (plastics, resins, mastics, roofing felts, vinyl floor tiles, semi-rigid paints or decorative finishes, asbestos cement etc) scores 1.

In the material assessment, a product type (or debris from product) of AIB, millboards, other low-density insulation boards, asbestos textiles, gaskets, ropes and woven textiles, asbestos paper and felt scores 2.
In the material assessment, a product type (or debris from product) of thermal insulation (eg pipe and boiler lagging), sprayed asbestos, loose asbestos, asbestos mattresses and packing scores 3.
In the material assessment, extent of damage/deterioration scores 0 for good condition: no visible damage.
In the material assessment, extent of damage/deterioration scores 1 for low damage: a few scratches or surface marks, broken edges on boards, tiles etc.

In the material assessment, extent of damage/deterioration scores 2 for medium damage: significant breakage of materials or several small areas where material has been damaged revealing loose asbestos fibres.
In the material assessment, extent of damage/deterioration scores 3 for high damage or delamination of materials, sprays and thermal insulation, or visible asbestos debris.
In the material assessment, surface treatment scores 0 for composite materials containing asbestos: reinforced plastics, resins, vinyl tiles.
In the material assessment, surface treatment scores 1 for enclosed sprays and lagging, AIB (with exposed face painted or encapsulated) and asbestos cement sheets etc.
In the material assessment, surface treatment scores 2 for unsealed AIB, or encapsulated lagging and sprays.
In the material assessment, surface treatment scores 3 for unsealed lagging and sprays.
In the material assessment, an asbestos type of chrysotile scores 1.
In the material assessment, an asbestos type of amphibole asbestos excluding crocidolite scores 2.
In the material assessment, an asbestos type of crocidolite scores 3.
In the material assessment, a total score of 10 or more means a high potential to release asbestos fibres.
In the material assessment, a total score of 7-9 means a medium potential to release asbestos fibres.
In the material assessment, a total score of 5-6 means a low potential to release asbestos fibres.
In the material assessment, a total score of 4 or less means a very low potential to release asbestos fibres.

fixes.target: figure-1: Summary of the main steps in managing asbestos
fixes.value: Flowchart of the main steps in managing asbestos in a building. First appoint a person to manage asbestos and find out if asbestos-containing materials (ACMs) are present by checking plans or drawings and carrying out a survey; if none are found, record it and take no further action. If they are found, prepare an asbestos register and plan or drawing, carry out a risk assessment (are ACMs likely to be disturbed, who could be exposed, what comes first), then prepare a management plan: monitor ACMs in good condition, repair or remove damaged ones, and manage maintenance work (train staff, manage contractors, check work against the plan, follow Asbestos essentials and CAR).
fixes.reason: Short description for search, from the figure image, caption and labels only.

fixes.target: figure-2: Schematic diagram showing the link between the asbestos survey and the management plan
fixes.value: Diagram showing how an asbestos survey leads to the management plan. A survey is either a management survey or a refurbishment or demolition survey, and both feed the asbestos register and plan or drawing. The register leads to a risk assessment, and the risk assessment leads to the management plan.
fixes.reason: Short description for search, from the figure image, caption and labels only.
